title: The Voice From IT
setting: a casino's help desk at night

post.author: u/castellane_desk_itzel
post.title: I run a casino's night help desk. At 02:40 we reset our finance manager's sign-in, exactly by the book. She was asleep, and she had called nobody.

blocks.text: I'm Itzel, night lead on the help desk at the Castellane, a casino that never closes. A help desk is the team staff ring when a computer or a sign-in stops working. Our nights run 20:00 to 08:00; a day team covers the rest, under the same written policy.
Staff sign in with a password and a second proof: a code from an app on their own phone. Asking for two different kinds of proof is called multi-factor sign-in, or MFA (as in Who Are You).

Phones get lost or replaced, so the desk can reset a sign-in. First, the agent wipes the old second proof. Second, the agent gives the caller a temporary password. Third, the next device to sign in with it registers a new second proof, and is trusted from then on.

Before a reset, our policy says the agent asks three personal questions, with answers from the caller's staff record. Three right answers, reset done. Some accounts are privileged: they can do more, such as approving payments. 41 of our 1,380 staff accounts are.
In the 30 days to 08:00 this morning, Monday 12 October, the desk did 214 resets. 11 were on privileged accounts, and 61 happened at night.

Sunday was my night off. Szabina had the desk alone, 20:00 to 08:00. At 02:40 a caller said she was Ms Ojukwu, our finance manager, locked out and in a hurry. The caller answered all three questions, and Szabina reset the account. It was the night's only reset.

At 07:10 Ms Ojukwu rang the desk herself: the app on her phone had stopped working. She had been asleep at 02:40 and had rung nobody. Her mobile number has been on her staff file since she joined, in March 2023. Szabina rang me at 07:15, and I came in.
Below is her account's log for the night. Each line shows the time, what happened, and the agent's note where there is one.

Mon 12 Oct 02:40  reset: second proof wiped, temporary password given   agent Szabina: 3 questions, 3 right
Mon 12 Oct 02:51  sign-in from a device never seen before; new second proof registered
Mon 12 Oct 02:52  supplier payment records opened
Mon 12 Oct 03:20  signed out
Mon 12 Oct 07:10  sign-in failed: code from her own phone refused

Nothing warned anyone overnight: no rule watches resets. Every line is valid: the right answers, a proper reset, a proper sign-in. So far we find nothing changed in the payment records. Szabina followed the policy to the letter.

blocks.label: ojukwu_account_night_11_oct.png

diagram.aria: The night shift from 20:00 on Sunday 11 October to 08:00 on Monday 12 October. The desk is staffed all night. Ms Ojukwu's phone holds her second proof until 02:40, when the reset wipes it; from then until her call at 07:10 her phone's code no longer works. A device never seen before is signed in to her account from 02:51 to 03:20.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the reset log and her sign-in log. The desk was staffed all night, 20:00 to 08:00. At 02:40 the reset wiped the second proof on Ms Ojukwu's phone; at 02:51 a device never seen before signed in as her and stayed until 03:20. She found out at 07:10, when her own code was refused.

blocks.text: The door was locked. We opened it ourselves, politely, for a voice.

Our security officer put names to it this morning. Vishing is a phone call from someone who is not who they claim; it works because a colleague in trouble makes people want to help. Pretexting is the made-up reason for the call; it works because the reason fits what the listener expects to hear.

She also wants every staff member on passkeys: a sign-in key kept on your own phone and unlocked with your fingerprint. A passkey answers only the casino's real sign-in page, so a fake copy of the page gets nothing from it.
The policy review is on Thursday, and I get one change to propose. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: What you're describing has a name: account recovery, getting someone back in after they lose a proof. Before you choose, two questions. Three right answers prove the caller knows three facts about Ms Ojukwu; who else could know them? And who, besides the caller, heard about that reset before 07:10?

replies.author: u/castellane_desk_itzel
replies.text: Nobody heard. No rule tells anyone about a reset, and her phone showed nothing until the code failed at 07:10. The answers come from her staff record, which the agent sees on screen.

comments.author: u/twenty_years_on_phones_zoltan
comments.text: I trained call-centre agents for twenty years. A good agent can tell a fake caller: the pauses, the wrong words. Your questions are simply too easy. Add three harder ones and teach your people to listen. Ring every finance manager at 02:40 over a lost phone and you'll be very unpopular.

comments.author: u/castellane_nights_szabina
comments.text: I'm the agent. I did what the policy says, and the caller sounded exactly like someone locked out. If the rule had told me to do anything else, I would have done it.

reply.prompt: The policy review is on Thursday. What one change should Itzel propose? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add three more personal questions to the reset call, so a caller must know far more.
options.part2: We added three questions, six in all. In the sim I set six personal questions and ran the 30 days. All 214 resets are still done, no owner is reached on their own phone, and agent minutes double, from 642 to 1,284. The 02:40 reset goes through on 6 answers, and a new device signs in at 02:51. More questions ask for more facts about a person; none of them rings the person.
options.senior: Personal questions test what a caller knows, not who they are, and facts about a person can often be found or guessed. Adding more of them costs every honest caller time and barely slows a prepared one. Agents can't reliably hear a lie either; a calm, plausible voice is the whole point of vishing. Check through a route the caller doesn't control instead: ring the number already on file.

options.text: Before any reset, call the staff member back on the number already on their file.
options.part2: From Thursday, before any reset the agent rings the number already on the staff member's file, never the number calling, and resets only if the owner confirms. In the sim I chose call back on the number on file and ran the 30 days. At 02:40 Ms Ojukwu's own phone rings, she has asked for nothing, and the reset stops: no new device, nothing to clean up. 198 owners were reached on their own phones: 197 resets went ahead after the owner confirmed, and 1 stopped. 16 staff whose phones were lost were held for a badge check at the security desk. It costs time: 1,498 agent minutes in the 30 days instead of 642, 7 a reset. We added a second approver for privileged resets (1,542 minutes in all) and a warning to the duty manager whenever a reset is followed by a new device.
options.senior: Account recovery is the back door of every sign-in, so check it through a route the caller does not control. Ring the person on the number on file, set before the request, never the number they give; reset only when that person confirms. Guard the number on file just as well: change it only through the same strong check, and tell the old number. Add a second approver for privileged accounts and a warning when a reset is followed by a new device, and tell the owner every time. NIST's guidance says account recovery "SHALL cause a notification to be sent to the subscriber".

options.text: Move staff to passkeys on their own phones, which answer only the real sign-in page.
options.part2: Passkeys went on every staff phone. In the sim I turned passkeys on and kept the three questions. The 02:40 reset is still done, because a reset wipes the passkey too, and the new device at 02:51 registers its own. Passkeys stop fake sign-in pages, which is worth a lot, but this night never needed one: the desk opened the door.
options.senior: Passkeys are among the strongest everyday sign-ins: they answer only the real site, so a fake page gets nothing, and CISA and the FBI recommend phishing-resistant sign-in of this kind. Do it. But any sign-in is only as strong as the way back in after it is lost. If one phone call can wipe a passkey and let a new device register its own, the passkey protects everything except the reset. Fix the recovery check as well.

options.text: Ban resets at night, so any reset request must wait for the day team to handle it.
options.part2: Resets now wait for the day team. In the sim I held night resets: 61 of the 214 waited until morning. The 02:40 request waited too, and at 08:20 the day team reset it on the same three answers; a new device signed in at 08:31. The day team runs the same policy, so the night only moved the reset to breakfast time.
options.senior: The hour wasn't the weakness; the check was. Daytime brings more people nearby, not a better check, and 61 honest staff a month would wait hours to start a shift. A pretext works just as well at 08:20. Change what the agent checks, at every hour, and keep a warning running so an odd reset at any time reaches a person who can act.

sim.title: Replay 30 days of resets at the Castellane's help desk
sim.lede: You're Itzel, replaying every reset from 08:00 on Saturday 12 September to 08:00 on Monday 12 October 2026. The figures are given data: 214 resets, 11 on privileged accounts and 61 at night; row 214 is the 02:40 reset on Ms Ojukwu's account, followed at 02:51 by a device never seen before. Choose the identity check, a second approver for privileged accounts, number matching, passkeys, a warning when a reset is followed by a new device within 60 minutes, and whether night resets wait for the day team, then run the 30 days. Each row shows its check and outcome, never what was said on a call.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run the 30 days as found: all 214 resets done, no owner reached, and the 02:40 reset goes through on 3 answers. Try 6 questions: the same outcome for 1,284 agent minutes. Now choose call back on the number on file: at 02:40 her own phone rings and the reset stops; 198 owners reached, 16 held for a badge check. Turn on passkeys or number matching with the old questions: 02:40 is unchanged. Hold night resets: it happens at 08:20 instead. Last, turn on the warning: 151 warnings a month, and the account is suspended at 02:58.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke in. The help desk's policy let anyone who knew three facts from a staff record have a sign-in reset, and a reset wipes the second proof so the next device can register its own. The fix is to check through a route the caller does not control: call the person back on the number already on file, add a second approver for privileged accounts, warn on a reset followed by a new device, and tell the owner every time.

steps.title: Why a reset is the weak point.
steps.text: Multi-factor sign-in asks for two kinds of proof, but people lose phones, so every system needs a way back in. That way back is account recovery, and here it was a reset. First, the agent wipes the old second proof. Second, a temporary password goes to the caller. Third, the next device to sign in registers a new second proof and is trusted from then on. Whoever passes the reset check therefore gets everything the two proofs were protecting. A sign-in is only as strong as its reset.

steps.title: Vishing and pretexting, from the defender's side.
steps.text: Vishing is social engineering by phone: someone calls pretending to be someone else, and it works because helpful people want to solve a colleague's problem quickly. Pretexting is the made-up reason that comes with it, chosen to fit what the listener expects, so nothing sounds odd. The defender's lesson is not to train agents to hear lies, which people usually do badly, but to make the check independent of how convincing the caller is.

steps.title: Call back on the number on file, step by step.
steps.text: First, the agent takes the request and says the desk will call back. Second, the agent looks up the number on the staff member's file, recorded before the request, and never uses a number the caller gives. Third, the agent rings it; the person who answers confirms they asked. If nobody answers, nothing is reset and the request waits. Fourth, only then does the reset go ahead, and a message goes to the owner saying it happened. What can go wrong: a lost phone means the number on file can't be reached, so the request waits for a badge check in person; and a number on file that is out of date reaches nobody, so keep it current, change it only through the same strong check, and tell the old number when it changes.

steps.title: A second approver, and a warning on reset then new device.
steps.text: For privileged accounts, those that can approve payments or change settings, a second person must agree before the reset. A second approver adds a second look, not a second source of truth: on the old questions they agreed on the same three answers, so pair them with the callback. Then watch the result. When a reset is followed by a new device within a set window, 60 minutes here, a warning goes to the duty manager, who rings the owner on file. Most of those warnings are honest staff with new phones, 151 a month here, so each check must be quick.

steps.title: Number matching and passkeys: what they stop, and what they don't.
steps.text: Number matching shows a number on the sign-in screen that must be typed into the app on the registered phone, so a person can't approve a prompt they didn't start. A passkey, built on the FIDO2 and WebAuthn standards, is a sign-in key on your own device that answers only the real site, so a fake page gets nothing. Both make sign-in much harder to fool. Neither helps once a reset has registered a new device: the number then goes to that device, and it holds its own passkey. Use them, and fix the reset check as well.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Thursday. Top row: a reset request from any caller at any hour; the help desk, which never rings the caller's number; the number on file, set before the request. Bottom row: the second approver for privileged accounts, who agrees with the desk; the owner's own phone, which the number on file rings and where the owner confirms; the warning check, which watches for a reset followed by a new device and rings the owner too.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Thursday. A reset request, from any caller at any hour, goes to the help desk, which finds the number on file, set before the request, and rings the owner's own phone; the reset goes ahead only if the owner confirms. A second approver agrees for privileged accounts. The warning check watches for a reset followed by a new device and rings the owner too. Replayed, the 02:40 reset stops at her own phone.

fix.title: The fix: call back on the number on file, a second approver for privileged accounts, and a warning on reset then new device
fix.text: Before any reset, the agent rings the number already on the staff member's file, never a number the caller gives, and resets only when the owner confirms; a staff member whose phone is lost proves who they are in person, with their badge, at the security desk. Changes to the number on file get the same strong check. Privileged accounts need a second approver as well. Every reset sends a message to the owner, and a reset followed by a new device within 60 minutes warns the duty manager, who rings the owner on file. Keep moving staff to passkeys and number matching, because they make sign-in itself much harder to fool. In the sim, call back on file stops the 02:40 reset at Ms Ojukwu's own phone; 198 owners are reached, 16 lost-phone resets wait for a badge check, and agent minutes rise from 642 to 1,498.

limits: A callback is only as good as the number on file. Keeping that number current, and changing it only through the same strong check with a message to the old number, becomes part of the job.
It costs time and people: 1,498 agent minutes in the 30 days instead of 642, and 16 staff with lost phones waiting for an in-person badge check before a shift.
The warning is noisy: 151 a month, almost all honest staff with new phones. It helps only if each check is quick and someone always answers it.

explain.seniorTake: Every sign-in has a way back in for people who lose a proof, and that way back decides how strong the sign-in really is. Help-desk resets are where people, not machines, decide, so design the check so a convincing voice is not enough: verify through a route the caller does not control, the number already on file, set before the request; give privileged accounts a second approver; tell the owner after every reset; and warn when a reset is followed by a new device. Then make sign-in itself harder to fool with number matching and passkeys, which answer only the real site. Don't ask agents to hear lies, and don't move the problem to another hour; change what the check relies on.

realWorld.title: CISA and FBI AA23-320A: the help desk as target
realWorld.text: The joint advisory on the group called Scattered Spider says, in its list of methods: "Scattered Spider threat actors use social engineering to convince IT helpdesk personnel to reset passwords and/or MFA tokens." An MFA token here means the second proof.

realWorld.title: CISA and FBI AA23-320A: the mitigation
realWorld.text: Among its mitigations: "Implement FIDO/WebAuthn authentication or Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)-based MFA." It says these are "resistant to phishing and not susceptible to push bombing or SIM swap attacks".

realWorld.title: Twitter, July 2020: callers posing as IT
realWorld.text: The New York State Department of Financial Services report, October 2020, says one or more hackers "called several Twitter employees and claimed to be calling from the Help Desk in Twitter’s IT department." Here the caller posed as IT; at the Castellane the caller posed as staff. Both rely on a help desk's trusted voice.

realWorld.title: Uber, September 2022: repeated prompts
realWorld.text: Uber's own update says nothing about anyone posing as IT. It says the contractor "received a two-factor login approval request, which initially blocked access. Eventually, however, the contractor accepted one". Number matching is built for that problem.

realWorld.title: Number matching, in Microsoft's documentation
realWorld.text: "When users respond to an MFA push notification by using Authenticator, they see a number. They need to enter that number into the app to complete the approval."

realWorld.title: WebAuthn: a credential tied to one site
realWorld.text: The W3C's Web Authentication Level 3 specification: "Subsequently, the public key credential can only be accessed by origins belonging to that Relying Party." In plain words, the key answers only the site it was made for.

realWorld.title: FIDO Alliance: passkeys resist phishing
realWorld.text: "Unlike passwords, passkeys are phishing-resistant, are always strong, and are designed so that there are no shared secrets."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-63B: tell the owner
realWorld.text: On account recovery: "In all cases, account recovery SHALL cause a notification to be sent to the subscriber or their designee, as described in Sec. 4.6."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.17, from a guide
realWorld.text: The standard is paid, so this is ISMS.online's guide, not the standard: "Organisations should have solid processes to check a user's identity before they are given new or replacement authentication" information.

asked: How do you secure account recovery?
What is number matching, and what does it stop?
interview.answer: Account recovery is the way back in when someone loses a proof, and it is usually the weakest part of sign-in, because a person decides. Secure it by checking through a route the caller does not control: call back on a number or address already on file, recorded before the request, and never on one the caller gives; guard changes to that number just as strongly. Add a second approver for privileged accounts, send the owner a message after every recovery, as NIST SP 800-63B requires, and warn when a recovery is followed by a new device. Avoid personal questions: they test knowledge that is often findable. Phishing-resistant sign-in, such as FIDO2 and WebAuthn passkeys, ties the key to the real site, so a fake page gets nothing and there is no code to read out. Number matching makes the person type a number shown on the sign-in screen into their app, which stops them approving a prompt they didn't start; it does nothing once a reset has registered a new device. A story I'd tell: a casino's help desk reset its finance manager's second proof at 02:40 on three personal questions while she slept; a callback on her number on file would have rung her own phone.

Getting someone back into an account after they lose a proof, such as a phone. A help-desk reset is one way. It is often the weakest part of sign-in.

An account that can do more than most, such as approving payments or changing settings. Ms Ojukwu's is one of the Castellane's 41.
The phone number recorded on a staff member's file before any request. Ms Ojukwu's mobile has been on hers since March 2023.
Ending the call and ringing the person on the number already on their file, never one the caller gives, and resetting only if they confirm.

Tricking someone into giving a password or code, often with a fake copy of a real sign-in page.
Sign-in that a fake page cannot trick, because the key answers only the real site. Passkeys built on FIDO2 and WebAuthn are phishing-resistant.
A set of open standards from the FIDO Alliance for signing in with keys on your own device instead of passwords. Passkeys are built on it.
Short for Web Authentication: the W3C standard that lets websites use keys on your device to sign you in. Each key is tied to one site.
An industry group that publishes the FIDO standards for signing in without passwords, including passkeys.
Short for World Wide Web Consortium: the body that publishes web standards, including WebAuthn.
The sign-in screen shows a number that must be typed into the app on the registered phone, so nobody approves a prompt they didn't start.
Sending sign-in prompts again and again in the hope that one gets accepted. Number matching is built to stop it.
Moving someone's phone number to a new SIM card without their consent, so codes sent by text go to the wrong phone. Passkeys don't rely on texts.
Short for public key infrastructure: a system of digital certificates that proves who holds which key. CISA lists PKI-based sign-in beside FIDO and WebAuthn.
WebAuthn's name for the website or service a key is made for. The key answers only that site's own addresses, called its origins.
The name CISA and the FBI use for a criminal group that targets large companies and their IT help desks, described in advisory AA23-320A.

The manager on shift through the night at the Castellane, who acts as second approver and answers warnings about resets.

A phone, tablet or computer used to sign in. After a reset, the next new device registers the second proof and is trusted.

atWork: Find your help desk's written steps for resetting a password or a second proof, and read them as a stranger would. It is a common pattern: a reset after a few personal questions answered from an HR record, with nobody told afterwards. Ask four things. Does the check go through a route the caller doesn't control, such as a call back on a number already on file? Who can change that number, and how? Do privileged accounts need a second approver? Does the owner always hear about a reset, and does anyone get warned when a reset is followed by a new device? Check outside support firms too: their copy of the steps must match yours. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.5.17 (authentication information) expects identity to be checked before authentication information is issued or reset, A.8.5 covers secure authentication, and A.6.3 covers awareness training for staff such as the help desk; if SOC 2, criterion CC6.2 covers how users' access is registered and changed. NIST SP 800-63B's account recovery section, which requires a notification after every recovery, is a good model either way. Build it in now, with a dated record of each reset, its check and its outcome, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's IT help desk resets a staff member's sign-in, wiping the second proof, after the caller answers questions from the HR record. An auditor asks how you secure account recovery. What do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Check through a route the caller doesn't control: call back on the number already on file
Privileged accounts need a second approver
Warn when a reset is followed by a new device, and tell the owner after every reset

recall.model: Personal questions test what a caller knows, and facts about a person can often be found, so stop relying on them. First, before any reset, end the call and ring the staff member back on the number already on file, recorded before the request, never one the caller gives; reset only if they confirm, and guard changes to that number just as strongly. Second, for privileged accounts, require a second approver as well. Third, notify the owner after every reset, and warn the duty team when a reset is followed by a new device, so a wrong one is caught in minutes.

options: It is longer than a password
It answers only the real site it was made for, so a fake page gets nothing
The help desk keeps a copy
recall.why: A passkey is tied to one site: WebAuthn says the credential can only be accessed by origins belonging to that site. A fake copy of the page is a different site, so the key gives it nothing, and there is no code for a person to read out.

recall.prompt: What does number matching stop, and what doesn't it stop?
options: It stops every kind of account takeover
It stops approving a prompt you didn't start, but not a reset that registers a new device
It stops resets, but not fake pages
It stops nothing; it only slows sign-in
recall.why: You must type the number shown on the sign-in screen, so a blind approval of a prompt you didn't start fails. After a reset, though, the prompt goes to the newly registered device, so number matching can't help there.

recall.prompt: In the sim, why did six personal questions still let the 02:40 reset through?
options: They test facts about a person, not the person, and never reach the owner's own phone
Six is too few; ten would have worked
Questions only work in the daytime
recall.why: Every question asks for a fact, and facts about a person can often be found. With six questions no owner is reached in the 30 days and agent minutes double to 1,284; only a call back on the number on file reached Ms Ojukwu.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The call back has run every night since October, and no reset has gone through without its owner. In February the Castellane handed weekend nights to an outside support company to save money. Last night, at 03:05 on Sunday 14 March, its agent reset a pit boss's sign-in, a privileged account, after three personal questions: the company's own written steps had never been updated. A device never seen before signed in at 03:16. The pit boss was asleep. Nobody at the casino knew until his phone's code failed at 09:00.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How did the old gap come back, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The casino's reset rule must bind whoever runs the desk: written into the agreement and checked
Privileged resets need the casino's own second approver, whoever takes the call
Warn on a reset followed by a new device, and tell the owner, wherever the reset happens

coldCase.model: The gap came back through the supplier: the casino changed its own steps but not the outside company's, and a reset done by a third party is still a reset of the casino's accounts. First, write the call back on file into the contract, as the same policy, and check it with spot reviews of their reset log. Second, make privileged resets need the casino's own second approver, the duty manager, whoever takes the call. Third, run the warning on a reset followed by a new device across every reset, wherever it is done, and notify the owner each time, so a pit boss hears at 03:05, not at 09:00.
